{{Short description|Programming language evaluation rules}}
{{CS1 config|mode=cs1}}
{{Evaluation strategy}}

In a [[programming language]], an '''evaluation strategy''' is a set of rules for evaluating [[Expression (computer science) | expressions]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Araki |first1=Shota |last2=Nishizaki |first2=Shin-ya |chapter=Call-by-name evaluation of RPC and RMI calculi |title=Theory and Practice of Computation |date=November 2014 |page=1 |doi=10.1142/9789814612883_0001 |isbn=978-981-4612-87-6 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MFMCCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA1 |access-date=21 August 2021}}</ref> The term is often used to refer to the more specific notion of a ''parameter-passing strategy''<ref>{{cite book |last1=Turbak |first1=Franklyn |last2=Gifford |first2=David |title=Design Concepts in Programming Languages |date=18 July 2008 |publisher=MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-30315-6 |page=309 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9yw3AgAAQBAJ&pg=PA309 |language=en}}</ref> that defines the kind of value that is passed to the function for each parameter (the ''binding strategy'')<ref>{{cite conference |last1=Crank |first1=Erik |last2=Felleisen |first2=Matthias |book-title=Proceedings of the 18th ACM SIGPLAN-SIGACT symposium on Principles of programming languages - POPL '91 |title=Parameter-passing and the lambda calculus |date=1991 |page=2 |citeseerx=10.1.1.23.4385 |doi=10.1145/99583.99616 |isbn=0897914198 |s2cid=5782416}}</ref> and whether to evaluate the [[Parameter (computer science)|parameters]] of a function call, and if so in what order (the ''evaluation order'').<ref name="Wilhelm">{{cite book |last1=Wilhelm |first1=Reinhard |last2=Seidl |first2=Helmut |title=Compiler Design: Virtual Machines |date=10 November 2010 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-3-642-14909-2 |page=61 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kDYueCmZLboC&pg=PA61 |language=en}}</ref> The notion of [[reduction strategy]] is distinct,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Nita |first1=Stefania Loredana |last2=Mihailescu |first2=Marius |title=Practical Concurrent Haskell |chapter=Introduction |date=2017 |page=3 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4842-2781-7_1 |isbn=978-1-4842-2780-0 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ydo1DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA3}}</ref> although some authors conflate the two terms and the definition of each term is not widely agreed upon.<ref name="Pierce">{{cite book |last=Pierce |first=Benjamin C. |author-link=Benjamin C. Pierce |title=Types and Programming Languages |year=2002 |publisher=[[MIT Press]] |isbn=0-262-16209-1 |page=56 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ti6zoAC9Ph8C&pg=PA56}}</ref> A programming language's evaluation strategy is part of its high-level [[Semantics (computer science)|semantics]]. Some languages, such as [[PureScript]], have variants with different evaluation strategies. Some [[declarative language]]s, such as [[Datalog]], support multiple evaluation strategies.

Just like in mathematics, evaluation is the process of finding the value corresponding to an expression.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |encyclopedia=[[Oxford English Dictionary]] |doi=10.1093/OED/3423541985 |title=Evaluate (v.), sense a |date=2023 |quote=Mathematics. To work out the ‘value’ of (a quantitative expression); to find a numerical expression for (any quantitative fact or relation).}}</ref><ref>{{cite encyclopedia |encyclopedia=[[Oxford English Dictionary]] |doi=10.1093/OED/1018661347 |title=Simplify (v.), sense 4.a |date=2023 |quote=To express (an equation or other mathematical expression) in a form that is easier to understand, analyse, or work with, e.g. by collecting like terms or substituting variables.}}</ref>

The [[calling convention]] consists of the low-level platform-specific details of parameter passing.

== Example ==
To illustrate, executing a function call <code>f(a, b)</code> may first evaluate the arguments <code>a</code> and <code>b</code>, store the results in [[Reference (computer science)|reference]]s or memory locations <code>ref_a</code> and <code>ref_b</code>, then evaluate the function's body with those references passed in. This gives the function the ability to look up the original argument values passed in through dereferencing the parameters (some languages use specific operators to perform this), to modify them via [[Assignment (computer science)|assignment]] as if they were local variables, and to return values via the references. This is the call-by-reference evaluation strategy.<ref>{{cite book |author1=Daniel P. Friedman |author2=Mitchell Wand |title=Essentials of Programming Languages |date=2008 |publisher=[[MIT Press|The MIT Press]] |location=Cambridge, MA |isbn=978-0262062794 |edition=third}}</ref>

== Evaluation orders ==
While the [[order of operations]] defines the [[abstract syntax tree]] of the expression, the evaluation order defines the order in which expressions are evaluated. For example, the Python program
<syntaxhighlight lang="python">
def f(x):
    print(x, end="")
    return x

print(f(1) + f(2))
</syntaxhighlight>
outputs <code>123</code> due to Python's left-to-right evaluation order, but a similar program in [[OCaml]]:
<syntaxhighlight lang="ocaml">
let f x = print_int x; x ;;
print_int (f 1 + f 2)
</syntaxhighlight>
outputs <code>213</code> due to OCaml's right-to-left evaluation order.

The evaluation order is mainly visible in code with [[Side effect (computer science)|side effects]], but it also affects the performance of the code because a rigid order inhibits [[instruction scheduling]]. For this reason language standards such as C++ traditionally left the order unspecified, although languages such as Java and C# define the evaluation order as left-to-right<ref name="Pragmatics"/>{{rp|240–241}} and the [[C++17]] standard has added constraints on the evaluation order.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Filipek |first1=Bartlomiej |title=Stricter Expression Evaluation Order in C++17 |url=https://www.cppstories.com/2021/evaluation-order-cpp17/ |website=C++ Stories |date=16 August 2021 |access-date=24 August 2021 |language=en-us}}</ref>

=== Strict evaluation <span class="anchor" id="Applicative order"></span> <span class="anchor" id="Eager evaluation"></span> ===

'''Applicative order''' is a family of evaluation orders in which a function's arguments are evaluated completely before the function is applied.
<ref name="SICP">{{cite book |last1=Abelson |first1=Harold |author1-link=Hal Abelson |last2=Sussman |first2=Gerald Jay |author2-link=Gerald Jay Sussman |date=1996 |title=Structure and interpretation of computer programs |publisher=[[MIT Press]] |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts |isbn=0-262-01153-0 |edition=2nd |url=http://mitpress.mit.edu/sicp/full-text/book/book.html |chapter=Normal Order and Applicative Order |chapter-url=https://mitpress.mit.edu/sites/default/files/sicp/full-text/book/book-Z-H-27.html#%_sec_4.2.1 |access-date=2006-03-06 |archive-date=2005-03-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050302014035/http://mitpress.mit.edu/sicp/full-text/book/book.html |url-status=dead }} See also footnote Temp 576.</ref> This has the effect of making the function [[Strict function|strict]], i.e. the function's result is undefined if any of the arguments are undefined, so applicative order evaluation is more commonly called '''strict evaluation'''. Furthermore, a function call is performed as soon as it is encountered in a procedure, so it is also called '''eager evaluation''' or '''greedy evaluation'''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Reese |first1=Richard M. |title=Learning Java Functional Programming |date=14 October 2015 |publisher=Packt Publishing Ltd |isbn=978-1-78528-935-4 |page=106 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cgKACwAAQBAJ&pg=PA106 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Antani |first1=Ved |last2=Timms |first2=Simon |last3=Mantyla |first3=Dan |title=JavaScript: Functional Programming for JavaScript Developers |date=31 August 2016 |publisher=Packt Publishing Ltd |isbn=978-1-78712-557-5 |page=614 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=n23WDQAAQBAJ&pg=PA614 |language=en}}</ref> Some authors refer to strict evaluation as "call by value" due to the call-by-value binding strategy requiring strict evaluation.<ref name="Wilhelm"/>

[[Common Lisp]], [[Eiffel (programming language)|Eiffel]] and Java evaluate function arguments left-to-right. C leaves the order undefined.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Seacord |first1=Robert C. |title=EXP30-C. Do not depend on the order of evaluation for side effects |url=https://wiki.sei.cmu.edu/confluence/display/c/EXP30-C.+Do+not+depend+on+the+order+of+evaluation+for+side+effects |website=SEI CERT C Coding Standard |publisher=Carnegie Mellon University |access-date=23 August 2021}}</ref> Scheme requires the execution order to be the sequential execution of an unspecified permutation of the arguments.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Anglade |first1=S. |last2=Lacrampe |first2=J. J. |last3=Queinnec |first3=C. |title=Semantics of combinations in scheme |journal=ACM SIGPLAN Lisp Pointers |date=October 1994 |volume=VII |issue=4 |pages=15–20 |doi=10.1145/382109.382669 |s2cid=2987427 |url=https://pages.lip6.fr/Christian.Queinnec/PDF/orleans.pdf}}</ref> [[OCaml]] similarly leaves the order unspecified, but in practice evaluates arguments right-to-left due to the design of its [[abstract machine]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Why are OCaml function arguments evaluated right-to-left? |url=https://discuss.ocaml.org/t/why-are-ocaml-function-arguments-evaluated-right-to-left/1214 |website=OCaml |language=en |date=30 November 2017}}</ref> All of these are strict evaluation.

===Non-strict evaluation <span class="anchor" id="Normal order"></span>===
A '''non-strict evaluation order''' is an evaluation order that is not strict, that is, a function may return a result before all of its arguments are fully evaluated.<ref name=Tremblay>{{cite journal |last1=Tremblay |first1=G. |title=Lenient evaluation is neither strict nor lazy |journal=Computer Languages |date=April 2000 |volume=26 |issue=1 |pages=43–66 |doi=10.1016/S0096-0551(01)00006-6 |citeseerx=10.1.1.137.9885}}</ref>{{rp|46–47}} The prototypical example is '''normal order evaluation''', which does not evaluate any of the arguments until they are needed in the body of the function.<ref>{{Cite thesis |url=https://collections.lib.utah.edu/ark:/87278/s6j69gxv/94159 |page=10 |title=Efficient evaluation of normal order through strictness information |date=March 1987 |publisher=University of Utah |last1=George |first1=Lai|type=MSc}}</ref> Normal order evaluation has the property that it terminates without error whenever any other evaluation order would have terminated without error.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Borning |first1=Alan |title=Applicative vs Normal Order Evaluation in Functional Languages |url=https://courses.cs.washington.edu/courses/cse505/99au/functional/applicative-normal.pdf |website=CSE 505: Concepts of Programming Languages |publisher=University of Washington |access-date=23 August 2021 |date=Autumn 1999}}</ref> The name "normal order" comes from the lambda calculus, where normal order reduction will find a normal form if there is one (it is a "normalizing" [[reduction strategy]]).<ref name="Mazzola">{{cite book |last1=Mazzola |first1=Guerino |last2=Milmeister |first2=Gérard |last3=Weissmann |first3=Jody |title=Comprehensive Mathematics for Computer Scientists 2 |date=21 October 2004 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-3-540-20861-7 |page=323 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SMWx5fQZcEUC&dq=applicative%20order%20normal%20order&pg=PA323 |language=en}}</ref> [[Lazy evaluation]] is classified in this article as a binding technique rather than an evaluation order. But this distinction is not always followed and some authors define lazy evaluation as normal order evaluation or vice-versa,<ref name="SICP"/><ref name="Sturm">{{cite book |last1=Sturm |first1=Oliver |title=Functional Programming in C#: Classic Programming Techniques for Modern Projects |date=11 April 2011 |publisher=John Wiley and Sons |isbn=978-0-470-74458-1 |page=91 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nOc-FYPXN9IC&pg=PA91 |language=en}}</ref> or confuse non-strictness with lazy evaluation.<ref name=Tremblay/>{{rp|43–44}}

Boolean expressions in many languages use a form of non-strict evaluation called [[short-circuit evaluation]], where evaluation evaluates the left expression but may skip the right expression if the result can be determined—for example, in a disjunctive expression (OR) where <code>true</code> is encountered, or in a conjunctive expression (AND) where <code>false</code> is encountered, and so forth.<ref name="Sturm"/> Conditional expressions similarly use non-strict evaluation - only one of the branches is evaluated.<ref name=Tremblay/>

===Comparison of applicative order and normal order evaluation===
With normal order evaluation, expressions containing an expensive computation, an error, or an infinite loop will be ignored if not needed,<ref name="Wilhelm"/> allowing the specification of user-defined control flow constructs, a facility not available with applicative order evaluation. Normal order evaluation uses complex structures such as [[thunk]]s for unevaluated expressions, compared to the [[call stack]] used in applicative order evaluation.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Marlow |first1=Simon |title=Why can't I get a stack trace? |url=https://wiki.haskell.org/HaskellImplementorsWorkshop/2012#Programme |website=Haskell Implementors Workshop 2012 |access-date=25 August 2021}}</ref> Normal order evaluation has historically had a lack of usable debugging tools due to its complexity.<ref>{{cite conference |last1=Nilsson |first1=Henrik |book-title=Proceedings of the fourth ACM SIGPLAN international conference on Functional programming |title=Tracing piece by piece: Affordable debugging for lazy functional languages |date=1999 |pages=36–47 |doi=10.1145/317636.317782 |isbn=1581131119 |citeseerx=10.1.1.451.6513|s2cid=13954359}}</ref>

== Strict binding strategies ==
===Call by value===
In call by value (or pass by value), the evaluated value of the argument expression is bound to the corresponding variable in the function (frequently by copying the value into a new memory region). If the function or procedure is able to assign values to its parameters, only its [[local variable]] is assigned—that is, anything passed into a function call is unchanged in the caller's [[scope (programming)|scope]] when the function returns. For example, in [[Pascal (programming language)|Pascal]], passing an array by value will cause the entire array to be copied, and any mutations to this array will be invisible to the caller:<ref>{{cite web |title=Open array parameters |url=https://www.freepascal.org/docs-html/ref/refsu68.html |website=www.freepascal.org |access-date=20 January 2024}}</ref>

<syntaxhighlight lang="pascal">
program Main;
uses crt;

procedure PrintArray(a: Array of integer);
var
  i: Integer;
begin
  for i := Low(a) to High(a) do
    Write(a[i]);
  WriteLn();
end;

Procedure Modify(Row : Array of integer);  
begin  
  PrintArray(Row); // 123
  Row[1] := 4;
  PrintArray(Row); // 143
end;

Var
  A : Array of integer; 
begin
  A := [1,2,3];
  PrintArray(A); // 123
  Modify(A);
  PrintArray(A); // 123
end.
</syntaxhighlight>

====Semantic drift====
Strictly speaking, under call by value, no operations performed by the called routine can be visible to the caller, other than as part of the return value.<ref name="CLU Reference Manual"/> This implies a form of [[purely functional programming]] in the implementation semantics. However, the circumlocution "call by value where the value is a reference" has become common in some languages, for example, the Java community.<ref name="Java is Pass-by-Value, Dammit!"/> Compared to traditional pass by value, the value which is passed is not a value as understood by the ordinary meaning of value, such as an integer that can be written as a literal, but an implementation-internal [[Reference (computer science)|reference]] handle. Mutations to this reference handle are visible in the caller. Due to the visible mutation, this form of "call by value" is more properly referred to as [[#Call by sharing|call by sharing]].<ref name="CLU Reference Manual"/>

In [[purely functional language]]s, values and data structures are immutable, so there is no possibility for a function to modify any of its arguments. As such, there is typically no semantic difference between passing by value and passing by reference or a pointer to the [[data structure]], and implementations frequently use call by reference internally for the efficiency benefits. Nonetheless, these languages are typically described as call by value languages.

===Call by reference===
Call by reference (or pass by reference) is an evaluation strategy where a parameter is bound to an implicit [[Reference (computer science)|reference]] to the variable used as argument, rather than a copy of its value. This typically means that the function can modify (i.e., [[Assignment (computer science)|assign to]]) the variable used as argument—something that will be seen by its caller. Call by reference can therefore be used to provide an additional channel of communication between the called function and the calling function. Pass by reference can significantly improve performance: calling a function with a many-megabyte structure as an argument does not have to copy the large structure, only the reference to the structure (which is generally a machine word and only a few bytes). However, a call-by-reference language makes it more difficult for a programmer to track the effects of a function call, and may introduce subtle bugs.

Due to variation in syntax, the difference between call by reference (where the reference type is implicit) and call by sharing (where the reference type is explicit) is often unclear on first glance. A simple litmus test is if it's possible to write a traditional <code>swap(a, b)</code> function in the language.<ref name="Java is Pass-by-Value, Dammit!">{{cite web
 |title=Java is Pass-by-Value, Dammit!
 |date=16 May 2001
 |url=http://javadude.com/articles/passbyvalue.htm
 |access-date=2016-12-24}}</ref> For example in Fortran:

<syntaxhighlight lang="fortran">
program Main
    implicit none
    integer :: a = 1
    integer :: b = 2
    call Swap(a, b)
    print *, a, b ! 2 1
contains
    subroutine Swap(a, b)
        integer, intent(inout) :: a, b
        integer :: temp
        temp = a
        a = b
        b = temp
    end subroutine Swap
end program Main
</syntaxhighlight>

Therefore, Fortran's <code>inout</code> intent implements call-by-reference; any variable can be implicitly converted to a reference handle. In contrast the closest one can get in Java is:
{{anchor|Java-box}}
<syntaxhighlight lang="java">
public class Main {
    static class Box {
        int value;
        public Box(int value) {
            this.value = value;
        }
    }

    static void swap(Box a, Box b) {
        int temp = a.value;
        a.value = b.value;
        b.value = temp;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Box a = new Box(1);
        Box b = new Box(2);
        swap(a, b);
        System.out.printf("a = %d, b = %d%n", a.value, b.value);
        // output: a = 2, b = 1
    }
}
</syntaxhighlight>

where an explicit <code>Box</code> type must be used to introduce a handle. Java is call-by-sharing but not call-by-reference.<ref name="Java is Pass-by-Value, Dammit!"/>

===Call by copy-restore===
Call by copy-restore—also known as "copy-in copy-out", "call by value result", "call by value return" (as termed in the [[Fortran]] community)—is a variation of call by reference. With call by copy-restore, the contents of the argument are copied to a new variable local to the call invocation. The function may then modify this variable, similarly to call by reference, but as the variable is local, the modifications are not visible outside of the call invocation during the call. When the function call returns, the updated contents of this variable are copied back to overwrite the original argument ("restored").<ref>{{cite web |last1=Coenen |first1=Frans |title=PARAMETER PASSING |url=https://cgi.csc.liv.ac.uk/~frans/OldLectures/2CS45/paramPassing/paramPassing.html#callByCopyRestore |website=cgi.csc.liv.ac.uk |access-date=22 January 2024}}</ref>

The semantics of call by copy-restore is similar in many cases to call by reference, but differs when two or more function arguments [[aliasing (computing)|alias]] one another (i.e., point to the same variable in the caller's environment). Under call by reference, writing to one argument will affect the other during the function's execution. Under call by copy-restore, writing to one argument will not affect the other during the function's execution, but at the end of the call, the values of the two arguments may differ, and it is unclear which argument is copied back first and therefore what value the caller's variable receives.<ref>{{cite book |chapter-url=https://www.lri.fr/~marche/MPRI-2-36-1/2012/poly-chap5.pdf |page=53|chapter=Call by Reference, Aliasing Issues|title=MPRI Course 2-36-1: Proof of Program (Lecture notes) |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240625131538/https://www.lri.fr/~marche/MPRI-2-36-1/2012/poly-chap5.pdf |archive-date=25 June 2024 }}</ref> For example, Ada specifies that the copy-out assignment for each {{code|in out}} or {{code|out}} parameter occurs in an arbitrary order.<ref>{{cite book |title=Ada 2022 Language Reference Manual |date=13 October 2023 |url=http://www.ada-auth.org/standards/22rm/RM-Final.pdf|page=215}}</ref> From the following program (illegal in Ada 2012)<ref>{{cite book |last1=Barnes |first1=John |title=Ada 2012 rationale: the language, the standard libraries |date=2013 |publisher=Springer |location=Heidelberg |isbn=978-3-642-45210-9|url=https://www.ada-europe.org/manuals/Rationale_2012.pdf|pages=15–16, 87–88}}</ref> it can be seen that the behavior of [[GNAT]] is to copy in left-to-right order on return:

<syntaxhighlight lang="ada">
with Ada.Text_IO; use Ada.Text_IO;

procedure Test_Copy_Restore is
  procedure Modify (A, B : in out Integer) is
  begin
      A := A + 1;
      B := B + 2;
  end Modify;
  X : Integer := 0;
begin
  Modify(X, X);
  Put_Line("X = " & Integer'Image(X));
end Test_Copy_Restore;
-- $ gnatmake -gnatd.E test_copy_restore.adb; ./test_copy_restore
-- test_copy_restore.adb:12:10: warning: writable actual for "A" overlaps with actual for "B" [-gnatw.i]
-- X = 2
</syntaxhighlight>

If the program returned 1 it would be copying right-to-left, and under call by reference semantics the program would return 3.

When the reference is passed to the caller uninitialized (for example an {{code|out}} parameter in Ada as opposed to an {{code|in out}} parameter), this evaluation strategy may be called "call by result".

This strategy has gained attention in [[multiprocessing]] and [[remote procedure call]]s,<ref name="rfc5531">{{cite journal |title=RPC: Remote Procedure Call Protocol Specification Version 2 |url=https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5531 |website=tools.ietf.org |date=May 2009 |publisher=IETF |access-date=7 April 2018 |last1=Thurlow |first1=Robert}}</ref> as unlike call-by-reference it does not require frequent communication between threads of execution for variable access.

===Call by sharing===
Call by sharing (also known as "pass by sharing", "call by object", or "call by object-sharing") is an evaluation strategy that is intermediate between call by value and call by reference. Rather than every variable being exposed as a reference, only a specific class of values, termed "references", "[[boxed type]]s", or "objects", have reference semantics, and it is the addresses of these pointers that are passed into the function. Like call by value, the value of the address passed is a copy, and direct assignment to the parameter of the function overwrites the copy and is not visible to the calling function. Like call by reference, mutating the target of the pointer is visible to the calling function. Mutations of a mutable object within the function are visible to the caller because the object is not copied or cloned&mdash;it is ''shared'', hence the name "call by sharing".<ref name="CLU Reference Manual"/>

The technique was first noted by [[Barbara Liskov]] in 1974 for the [[CLU (programming language)|CLU]] language.<ref name="CLU Reference Manual">{{cite web |last1=Liskov |first1=Barbara |last2=Atkinson |first2=Russ |last3=Bloom |first3=Toby |last4=Moss |first4=Eliot |last5=Schaffert |first5=Craig |last6=Scheifler |first6=Craig |last7=Snyder |first7=Alan |title=CLU Reference Manual |work=Laboratory for Computer Science |publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology |date=October 1979 |url=http://www.lcs.mit.edu/publications/pubs/pdf/MIT-LCS-TR-225.pdf |access-date=2011-05-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060922165201/http://www.lcs.mit.edu/publications/pubs/pdf/MIT-LCS-TR-225.pdf |archive-date=2006-09-22 |url-status=live |pages=14–15}}</ref> It is used by many modern languages such as [[Python (programming language)|Python]] (the shared values being called "objects"),<ref name="Lundh Call Object">{{cite web
 |last=Lundh
 |first=Fredrik
 |title=Call by Object
 |work=Effbot.org
 |url=http://effbot.org/zone/call-by-object.htm
 |access-date=2011-05-19
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110519060105/http://effbot.org/zone/call-by-object.htm
 |archive-date=2011-05-19
 |url-status=dead}}</ref> [[Java (programming language)|Java]] (objects), [[Ruby (programming language)|Ruby]] (objects), [[JavaScript]] (objects), Scheme (data structures such as vectors),<ref>{{cite web |last1=Jones |first1=Rhys Price |title=Is Scheme call-by-value? |url=http://www2.seas.gwu.edu/~rhyspj/spring10cs145/lab9/lab92.html |website=CS 145 Programming Languages Lab 9: Parameter Passing |publisher=George Washington University |access-date=20 January 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141016203925/http://www.seas.gwu.edu/~rhyspj/spring10cs145/lab9/lab92.html |archive-date=16 October 2014 |date=2010}}</ref> [[AppleScript]] (lists, records, dates, and script objects), OCaml and [[ML (programming language)|ML]] (references, records, arrays, objects, and other compound data types), [[Maple (software)|Maple]] (rtables and tables), and [[Tcl (programming language)|Tcl]] (objects).<ref>{{cite web |title=Tcl Library Procedures - Tcl_Obj manual page |url=https://www.tcl.tk/man/tcl8.4/TclLib/Object.html |website=www.tcl.tk}}</ref> The term "call by sharing" as used in this article is not in common use; the terminology is inconsistent across different sources. For example, in the Java community, they say that Java is call by value.<ref name="Java is Pass-by-Value, Dammit!"/>

For [[immutable object]]s, there is no real difference between call by sharing and call by value, except if object identity is visible in the language. The use of call by sharing with mutable objects is an alternative to [[output parameter|input/output parameters]]: the parameter is not assigned to (the argument is not overwritten and object identity is not changed), but the object (argument) is mutated.<ref name=CA1021>{{cite web |url=http://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/ms182131.aspx |title=CA1021: Avoid out parameters |date=15 November 2016 |publisher=Microsoft}}</ref>

For example, in Python, lists are mutable and passed with call by sharing, so:
<syntaxhighlight lang="python">
def f(l: list[int]) -> None:
    l.append(1)

m: list[int] = []
f(m)
print(m)
</syntaxhighlight>
outputs <code>[1]</code> because the <code>append</code> method modifies the object on which it is called.

In contrast, assignments within a function are not noticeable to the caller. For example, this code binds the formal argument to a new object, but it is not visible to the caller because it does not mutate {{code|a_list}}:
<syntaxhighlight lang="python">
def f(l: list[int]) -> None:
    l = l + [1]
    print(l) # [1]

m: list[int] = []
f(m)
print(m) # []
</syntaxhighlight>

===Call by address===
{{anchor|call-by-address}}
'''Call by address''', pass by address, or call/pass by [[pointer (computer programming)|pointer]] is a parameter passing method where the address of the argument is passed as the formal parameter. Inside the function, the address (pointer) may be used to access or modify the value of the argument. For example, the swap operation can be implemented as follows in C:<ref>{{cite book |last1=Leo |first1=Ray |title=Little C++ (Made Easy) |date=November 1996 |publisher=LeoSudo Inc |isbn=978-0-9654634-1-6 |pages=79–80 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BK-yeUGlEqgC&dq=%22call%20by%20address%22%20%22call%20by%20pointer%22%20C%2B%2B&pg=PA79 |language=en}}</ref>

<syntaxhighlight lang="c">
#include <stdio.h>

void swap(int* a, int* b) {
    int temp = *a;
    *a = *b;
    *b = temp;
}

int main() {
    int a = 1;
    int b = 2;
    swap(&a, &b);
    printf("%d %d\n", a, b); // 2 1
    return 0;
}
</syntaxhighlight>

Some authors treat <code>&</code> as part of the syntax of calling {{code|swap}}. Under this view, C supports the call-by-reference parameter passing strategy.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Dandamudi |first1=Sivarama P. |title=Guide to Assembly Language Programming in Linux |date=15 July 2005 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-0-387-25897-3 |page=232 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wS4EG0GyKXUC&dq=c%20%22call%20by%20reference%22%20-%22c%2B%2B%22&pg=PA232 |language=en}}</ref> Other authors take a differing view that the presented implementation of {{code|swap}} in C is only a simulation of call-by-reference using pointers.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Srivastava |first1=S. K. |last2=Srivastava |first2=Deepali |title=C in Depth |date=6 June 2018 |publisher=BPB Publications |isbn=978-93-87284-94-4 |page=206 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IYxjDwAAQBAJ&dq=c%20%22call%20by%20reference%22%20-%22c%2B%2B%22&pg=PA206 |language=en}}</ref> Under this "simulation" view, mutable variables in C are not first-class (that is, l-values are not expressions), rather pointer types are. In this view, the presented swap program is [[syntactic sugar]] for a program that uses pointers throughout,<ref>{{cite web |title=Mutable Variables and Reference Types |url=https://okmij.org/ftp/meta-programming/mutable-var.html |website=okmij.org |access-date=20 January 2024}}</ref> for example this program ({{code|read}} and {{code|assign}} have been added to highlight the similarities to the Java {{code|Box}} call-by-sharing program [[#Java-box|above]]):

<syntaxhighlight lang="c">
#include <stdio.h>

int read(int* p) {
    return *p;
}

void assign(int* p, int v) {
    *p = v;
}

void swap(int* a, int* b) {
    int temp_storage; 
    int* temp = &temp_storage;
    assign(temp, read(a));
    assign(a, read(b));
    assign(b, read(temp));
}

int main() {
    int a_storage; 
    int* a = &a_storage;
    int b_storage; 
    int* b = &b_storage;
    assign(a, 1);
    assign(b, 2);
    swap(a, b);
    printf("%d %d\n", read(a), read(b)); // 2 1
    return 0;
}
</syntaxhighlight>

Because in this program, {{code|swap}} operates on pointers and cannot change the pointers themselves, but only the values the pointers point to, this view holds that C's main evaluation strategy is more similar to call-by-sharing.

C++ confuses the issue further by allowing {{code|swap}} to be declared and used with a very lightweight "reference" syntax:<ref>{{cite book |last1=Vermeir |first1=Dirk |title=Multi-Paradigm Programming using C++ |date=28 June 2011 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-1-4471-0311-0 |pages=10–11 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dW4QBwAAQBAJ&dq=%22call%20by%20address%22&pg=PA10 |language=en}}</ref>

<syntaxhighlight lang="c++">
void swap(int& a, int& b) {
    int temp = a;
    a = b;
    b = temp;
}

int main() {
    int a = 1;
    int b = 2;
    swap(a, b);
    std::println("{} {}", a, b); // 2 1
    return 0;
}
</syntaxhighlight>

Semantically, this is equivalent to the C examples. As such, many authors consider call-by-address to be a unique parameter passing strategy distinct from call-by-value, call-by-reference, and call-by-sharing.

===Call by unification===
In [[logic programming]], the evaluation of an expression may simply correspond to the [[Unification (computer science)|unification]] of the terms involved combined with the application of some form of [[Resolution (logic)|resolution]]. Unification must be classified as a strict binding strategy because it is fully performed. However, unification can also be performed on unbounded variables, so calls may not necessarily commit to final values for all its variables.

== Non-strict binding strategies ==
===Call by name===
Call by name is an evaluation strategy where the arguments to a function are not evaluated before the function is called—rather, they are substituted directly into the function body (using [[capture-avoiding substitution]]) and then left to be evaluated whenever they appear in the function. If an argument is not used in the function body, the argument is never evaluated; if it is used several times, it is re-evaluated each time it appears. (See [[Jensen's device]] for a programming technique that exploits this.)

Call-by-name evaluation is occasionally preferable to call-by-value evaluation. If a function's argument is not used in the function, call by name will save time by not evaluating the argument, whereas call by value will evaluate it regardless. If the argument is a non-terminating computation, the advantage is enormous. However, when the function argument is used, call by name is often slower, requiring a mechanism such as a [[Thunk (functional programming)#Call by name|thunk]].

[[List of CLI languages|.NET languages]] can simulate call by name using delegates or <code>Expression<T></code> parameters. The latter results in an [[abstract syntax tree]] being given to the function. [[Eiffel (programming language)|Eiffel]] provides agents, which represent an operation to be evaluated when needed. [[Java (programming language)|Java]] programs can accomplish similar lazy evaluation using [[Anonymous function|lambda expressions]] and the <code>java.util.function.Supplier<T></code> interface.

===Call by need===<!-- This section is linked from [[Functional programming]] -->
{{main|Lazy evaluation}}
Call by need is a [[memoization|memoized]] variant of call by name, where, if the function argument is evaluated, that value is stored for subsequent use. If the argument is [[Pure function|pure]] (i.e., free of side effects), this produces the same results as call by name, saving the cost of recomputing the argument.

[[Haskell]] is a well-known language that uses call-by-need evaluation. Because evaluation of expressions may happen arbitrarily far into a computation, Haskell supports only side effects (such as [[Mutable object|mutation]]) via the use of [[Monad (functional programming)|monads]]. This eliminates any unexpected behavior from variables whose values change prior to their delayed evaluation.

In [[R (programming language)|R]]'s implementation of call by need, all arguments are passed, meaning that R allows arbitrary side effects.

[[Lazy evaluation]] is the most common implementation of call-by-need semantics, but variations like [[#Optimistic evaluation|optimistic evaluation]] exist. [[List of CLI languages|.NET languages]] implement call by need using the type <code>Lazy<T></code>.

[[Graph reduction]] is an efficient implementation of lazy evaluation.

===Call by macro expansion===
Call by macro expansion is similar to call by name, but uses textual substitution rather than [[capture-avoiding substitution]]. Macro substitution may therefore result in variable capture, leading to mistakes and undesired behavior. [[Hygienic macros]] avoid this problem by checking for and replacing [[Variable shadowing|shadowed variables]] that are not parameters.

===Call by future===<!-- This section is linked from [[Functional programming]] -->
"Call by future", also known as "parallel call by name" or "lenient evaluation",<ref>{{cite web |last1=McCollin |first1=Thomas Gwynfryn |last2=Morell |first2=Tobias |title=A Game of Paradigms: A Usability Study of Functional Idioms in Gameplay Programming |url=https://projekter.aau.dk/projekter/files/306585571/PT103F19_report.pdf#page=12 |page=6 |publisher=Aalborg University |access-date=11 January 2022}}</ref> is a [[concurrent programming|concurrent]] evaluation strategy combining non-strict semantics with eager evaluation. The method requires fine-grained dynamic scheduling and synchronization but is suitable for massively parallel machines.

The strategy creates a [[futures and promises|future (promise)]] for the function's body and each of its arguments. These futures are computed [[Concurrency (computer science)|concurrently]] with the flow of the rest of the program. When a future A requires the value of another future B that has not yet been computed, future A blocks until future B finishes computing and has a value. If future B has already finished computing the value is returned immediately. Conditionals block until their condition is evaluated, and lambdas do not create futures until they are fully applied.<ref name="Schauser">{{cite conference |last1=Schauser |first1=Klaus E. |last2=Goldstein |first2=Seth C. |book-title=Proceedings of the seventh international conference on Functional programming languages and computer architecture - FPCA '95 |title=How much non-strictness do lenient programs require? |date=1995 |pages=216–225 |doi=10.1145/224164.224208 |isbn=0897917197 |s2cid=2045943 |url=http://www.cs.cmu.edu/~seth/papers/schauser-fplca95.pdf |access-date=7 January 2022}}</ref>

If implemented with processes or threads, creating a future will spawn one or more new processes or threads (for the promises), accessing the value will synchronize these with the main thread, and terminating the computation of the future corresponds to killing the promises computing its value. If implemented with a [[coroutine]], as in [[.NET]] [[async/await]], creating a future calls a coroutine (an async function), which may yield to the caller, and in turn be yielded back to when the value is used, cooperatively multitasking.

The strategy is non-deterministic, as the evaluation can occur at any time between creation of the future (i.e., when the expression is given) and use of the future's value. The strategy is non-strict because the function body may return a value before the arguments are evaluated. However, in most implementations, execution may still get stuck evaluating an unneeded argument. For example, the program
<syntaxhighlight lang="haskell">
f x = 1/x
g y = 1
main = print (g (f 0))
</syntaxhighlight>
may either have {{code|g}} finish before {{code|f}}, and output 1, or may result in an error due to evaluating {{code|1/0}}.<ref name=Tremblay/>

Call-by-future is similar to call by need in that values are computed only once. With careful handling of errors and nontermination, in particular terminating futures partway through if it is determined they will not be needed, call-by-future also has the same termination properties as call-by-need evaluation.<ref name="Schauser"/> However, call-by-future may perform unnecessary speculative work compared to call-by-need, such as deeply evaluating a lazy data structure.<ref name=Tremblay/> This can be avoided by using lazy futures that do not start computation until it is certain the value is needed.

===Optimistic evaluation===
Optimistic evaluation is a call-by-need variant where the function's argument is partly evaluated in a call-by-value style for some amount of time (which may be adjusted at [[Run time (program lifecycle phase)|runtime]]). After that time has passed, evaluation is aborted and the function is applied using call by need.<ref name="Optimistic Evaluation">{{cite conference
 |last1=Ennals |first1=Robert
 |last2=Peyton Jones |first2=Simon |author2-link=Simon Peyton Jones
 |title=Optimistic Evaluation: a fast evaluation strategy for non-strict programs 
 |conference=International Conference on Functional Programming
 |publisher=ACM Press
 |date=August 2003
 |url=https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/optimistic-evaluation-fast-evaluation-strategy-non-strict-programs/
 |url-status=dead
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250822195335/https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/optimistic-evaluation-fast-evaluation-strategy-non-strict-programs/
 |archive-date=22 August 2025}}</ref> This approach avoids some of call-by-need's runtime expenses while retaining desired termination characteristics.
